text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game: keeping tokens in my own account pays me fully but costs others, while putting tokens in the group account pays me a smaller amount but I need to figure out how it's shared among everyone.

Working through the math: my payoff equals my own tokens plus 0.75 times everyone's group contributions, including the loss from others keeping their tokens. Each token I keep nets me +0.25 regardless of what others do, so keeping all 20 is the dominant strategy — yet if everyone keeps all tokens, each person ends up with only 20 points, versus 60 points each if everyone fully contributes to the group. That's the classic social dilemma: individual rationality undermines collective payoff.

Since this repeats over 10 rounds and I only see group totals rather than individual contributions, conditional cooperation strategies are limited. For round 1, I'll open by contributing all 20 tokens to signal cooperative intent, then adjust based on how the group total responds.

This creates a classic cooperation dilemma where individually rational choices lead to a worse collective outcome.
